name: Microraptor
summary: Microraptor are tiny dromaeosaurids that utilize their wings to glide between trees and cliffs. Intelligent and ever cunning, Microraptor are capable of mimicking the calls of other species, which they use to their advantages in hunting and courtship.
credits: With contributions from: Kittyful, Red, YeahokayitsEDEN, CrownlessCrow, Zesty Filip
Profile inspired by rats, gray squirrels, sugar gliders, magpies, nazca boobies, and creative liberty.
quickView: Microraptor are Tiny Cathermal Terrestrial Carnivores.
Microraptor can group up to 10 sub/adults and unlimited offspring. Microraptor do not adopt as a rule, but same sex pairs within a scurry may adopt rejected chicks.
Microraptor can have up to 2 in a hunt, and 10 in a defence.
Microraptor may hunt attended or unattended Deinonychus, Latenivenatrix, Psittacosaurus, and Struthiomimus offspring of juvenile and below, and Rhamphorhynchus.
Microraptors are curious creatures with a unique gift in mimicking other species, a skill they use in both hunting and courtship.

Many Microraptors have vastly different preferences in the company they choose to keep, whereas more socially confident individuals choose to collect in large groups, known as scurries, those who prefer quieter lives remain with a pair, or completely solitary.

Microraptors, much like another familiar tiny-tier, find great company in other species, though lean heavily on the carnivorous variety. Oftentimes, this bond is one-sided, providing the Microraptor with far more advantages than it is able to return.

blocks.text: Tiny Cathemeral Terrestrial Carnivore Microraptor form temporary or harem bonds Some bonds may become lifelong, at the discretion of the individuals. Microraptor are territorial towards their own kind and claim territories consisting of their claimed tree, cliff ledge, or claimed carnivore companion. Microraptor have a tolerant nature. Microraptor are scavengers. Microraptor may opt to shun or tolerate mutated individuals, based on individual and group preference.

Skins that are considered mutations for Microraptor include: Albino, Melanistic, and all skins with "DRM" in the title. Players must roll in 🎲・genetics-rolls to use these skins in game. This is one roll per species, per character. Only when the character dies can you roll again if using the same character name.

Microraptor has optional subspecies differences, to match the places where they hatched. Microraptor with the Gui subspecies are born in: Redwoods, Hollow Hills, Wollemi Forest, East Passage, Twisted Forest, and Cedrus Forest. These individuals exhibit more stamina when climbing trees high distances. Microraptor with the Hanqiugi subspecies are born in: Dry Fang Canyon, Tallbrush Coasts, Crag Bluffs, Coastland Swamp, Mudflats, Coastal Bluffs, and Palm Islands. These individuals are able to go for longer without food and water. Microraptor with the Zhaoianus subspecies are born in Big Tree Overlook, Wind Tunnels, Cliff Edge Falls, Black Fern Hills, Volcano Islands and Stillwater Bog. These individuals are able to glide for longer. Gynandromorph Microraptor may perform either or both methods of courtship during the courtship period. The response they receive is up to the Microraptor they attempt to court. Gynandromorph individuals may never nest successfully.

Up to 10 Sub/Adults Unlimited Offspring Unlimited Adoptees Only same sex pairs in this group will adopt offspring. This group is known as a scurry. Scurries do not claim or follow other carnivore companions, and stick to their own species. or: Up to 2 Sub/Adults Unlimited Offspring This group type does not adopt. This group is known as a pair; they may choose to claim a carnivore companion. Solitary individuals may claim a carnivore companion. Microraptor may form dispersal groups of up to 10 individuals of Adolescent and below.

Predator Reaction: Flighty / Defensive Up to 2 Microraptor may work together in a hunt. Up to 10 Microraptor may react defensively when defending a claimed nesting site or when hunted. Microraptor flee from Hatzegopteryx, Quetzalcoatlus, Megalania, Kelenken, Thalassodromeus and Tropeognathus, unless nesting. When attacked by species they cannot hunt, solitary and pairs of Microraptor flee. Scurries who are attacked by species that they do not fear retaliate in the form of aggressive swarming. This behavior does not extend to Apex Carnivores. More information can be found under Cross Species Interaction.

Microraptor are primarily scavengers and insectivores, but may occasionally attempt to hunt. Microraptor can hunt attended or unattended Deinonychus, Latenivenatrix, Psittacosaurus, and Struthiomimus offspring of Juvenile and below. Microraptor may hunt Rhamphorhynchus. Microraptor are unable to eat the bodies of Metriacanthosaurus without suffering adverse side effects. See 📜・server-guideOPTIONAL - Illnesses & Injuries for more information.

🌧️ Rainy Season: 2 🥚 per 2 hours. ☀️ Dry Season: 2 🥚 per 2 hours. Microraptor nest in high up locations, such as cliffsides, ledges and treetops. Microraptor may form same-sex pairs but do not adopt unless as part of a scurry.
Microraptor do not have physical dimorphism.

Microraptor offspring, known as chicks, hatch out of their eggs burdened by their oversized wings. Damp, heavy, and entirely too large for their small body, any movement is quickly found to be far too tiring, resulting in long periods of rest. Offspring are assisted by their parents with constant preening and grooming, an action chicks appreciate heavily, as signified through their affectionate trills in between naps. Alongside keeping warm, a chick's top priority is ensuring they stay well fed. As soon as they sense a parent approaching, chicks scurry to the front of the nest and squall loudly for attention, pushing and shoving against their sibling in an effort to be fed first. As chicks age, they begin to notice a difference in attention provided towards themselves and their siblings. If a chick realizes itself to be favoured, and does not feel like sharing their parent’s affection, they may begin acting differently towards their sibling, shoving it about, and vocalizing in dissatisfaction, encouraging their parents to outcast it. Chicks may make this known by frequently bullying their sibling in front of their parents. Crying, screeching and aggressively wailing at their sibling, accompanied with shoving and pecks are common tactics. As chicks reach Juvenile, their bodies soon catch up with their wings, allowing for more movement. They begin stretching their wings, jumping and hopping around the perimeter of the nest, steadily increasing their strength in preparation for gliding. Chicks begin inquisitively playing with the various trinkets their parents gather for them, and often compete against their sibling to hoard particularly favoured items. This action may ignite scraps, though fights are never fatal. Once prompted by their parents, adolescent Microraptors will be pushed to leave the nest and begin gliding to other trees and cliffs nearby. They carefully aim for sturdy tree trunks, wide branches, and sturdy rocks, climbing to elevated heights to then practise gliding back to their nests. After considerable practice, chicks are deemed experienced enough to explore the world outside the nesting location. It’s at this point that parents lead offspring across various POIs, steadily introducing new items - and, most importantly, encouraging their offspring to begin mimicking other species they come across. As a Microraptor reaches Sub-Adult, offspring are steadily ushered into complete independence. If within a scurry, offspring generally choose to remain, though rarely interact with their parents aside from occasionally passing affectionate calls. Offspring that reach maturity within a pair grouping are made to disperse, first encouraged with gentle shoves, and then escalation to aggressive displays if the message is not made clear enough the first time.

Orphaned chicks often hatch on the forest floor, without the usual nest that provides warmth and safety during early stages of life. Chicks instinctively crawl towards safety, nestling between foliage or debris in an attempt to regulate their body temperature. Once a spot has been secured, the chick remains relatively stationary until Juvenile, practicing only minor movements during the few hours they are awake each day. These small bouts of exercise eventually build up, and as their need for continuous sleep decreases, chicks stray further and further away from their temporary nest, seeking out food, and eating near anything that they can grab with their beaks. These chicks are instinctively silent, lacking the parental figure needed to reinforce the idea that being loud is a rewarding behaviour. Due to having no positive association to outside noise, orphaned chicks treat unusual sounds as a potential threat. They are naturally skittish, and as a result, often sprint to the nearest dense bush or plentiful cover available to hide when they feel unfamiliar with a situation. Upon reaching adolescence, the orphaned chick is driven by compulsion to climb up nearby trees for safety and for better scouting opportunities. They cautiously glide from tree to tree, continuously seeking objects of interest, such as food, trinkets, other valuables, to find comfort in. The life of an orphaned Microraptor is not an easy one. Once the chick has reached Sub-Adult, they have typically gained enough confidence and mastered their basic survival skills to leave the grounds that raised them, and seek new lands to thrive in. Many orphaned Microraptors end up socially behind as adults, but offer unique habits that may be otherwise intriguing to others of their kind.

Microraptor are generally curious, but equally fearful creatures, perfectly capable of distinguishing when encounters may result in injury, and quick to disengage when that risk is present. These tiny dromeosaurids spend most of their time hopping and gliding from tree to tree or clinging to the edges of cliffs, observing their surroundings from a safe height. Microraptor are cautious, especially towards species they have never seen before. At the first sign of aggression towards them, they flee, typically accompanied with fearful cries. Microraptor are most commonly known for their mimicry of other species. When mimicking the call of a creature, they often call right back to the creature, very quickly memorizing the sound, and then repeating it in quick succession to familiarize themselves with the noise. Microraptor enjoy mimicking the calls of creatures in their surrounding area. When confronted by a species, and tolerated, Microraptor may take part in "conversations", in which they repeatedly parrot back calls made at them. Microraptor may go as far as to mimic the movement and actions of other species, though are quick to stop if agitation follows. Microraptor, for as small as they are, have an excellent memory, often recalling not only calls they’ve heard, but past experiences they have had with certain species. Microraptor have a general disdain for water, though are still regarded as clean creatures. Landing on sandy clearings and banks, Microraptor will use their small noses to toss sand around in order to take dust baths. Microraptor interact with any species that tolerates them, though do not linger long and do not form bond with any species other than Apex Carnivores.

Microraptor sleeps in short bursts - this is always high up in a tree or cliff. Caves and small tunnels are far too constricting and do not offer the creature the same freedom. Microraptor with carnivore companions who migrate often will cling to their sides, their heads falling forwards or to one side as they take the time to rest during travel. In scurries, all Microraptor take time to rest in unison. The group’s chatter fades into near silence as individuals drift to sleep. Some Microraptor may choose to remain alert while the group rests, quick to rouse the scurry if predators approach. Microraptor do not function in this way with their carnivore companions and are not sentries. They only react or alert to predators they must flee from.

Scurries are the most volatile of groupings for Microraptor, yet can also be one of the safest options. Scurries form naturally and often on a whim when lone Microraptor are not interested in searching for carnivore companions. Microraptor interested in grouping with others attempt to catch the attention of another with small chirps, landing hesitantly near them. If not aggressed out of their personal space immediately, the Microraptor shakes off the initial stress, and allows the other to approach cautiously, inspecting them with interest. If willing to accept the other, they both shake to loosen the initial tension and demonstrate friendliness. After this point, they may be accepted into the group. Any Microraptor may accept another into the scurry. Other members of the scurry who are nearby may also take part in the greeting and inspection. Should members of the scurry disagree with the choices of another, they will disperse from the scurry. Sometimes they may take more interest in the ungrouped individual, and chase after them in order to form a scurry of their own. Scurries can deny other Microraptor for any reason, which can lead to a constantly changing rotation of members. However, scurries with familial ties are less likely to have such experiences, and find it easier to maintain a consistent grouping. Within a scurry, there is no clear leader, and migrating can seem rather hectic, especially if there are several new individuals intent on proving themselves. Scurries often travel to the courtship grounds together, even if all members are not particularly interested in courting. New objects may be inspected by several members of a scurry at one time - however individual methods vary, often with the object being relocated frequently in a desperate attempt to get a better view. This action may spark disagreements if others feel they have not had adequate time to observe the object, inspiring short bursts of constant picking up and moving of the item around between scurry members. Vocal outbursts soon follow with prolonged bickering - though irritation never leads to biting. Many objects cannot be carried for long, as most are too heavy for the feeble Microraptor. Disagreements do not last long, as Microraptor eventually grow bored and move on to other activities.

Microraptor in pairs are able to enjoy the company of each other as well as that of Apex Carnivores. Pairs may consist of any relation between two Microraptor, guiding the direction of the interactions. Siblings are more prone to bickering over the smallest of issues - scraps of food, which side of a companion they're latched onto, or where to cross between POIs. Two uncourted individuals may only travel together briefly, benefiting from the company momentarily, but eventually going separate ways - or deciding to visit the courtship grounds together to make the bond official. Courted pairs are typically much more agreeable with each other and bicker far less, happily investigating objects together and exchanging mimicked calls to strengthen their bond. Pairs of Microraptor are more likely to remain with the same carnivore companion for longer than a solitary individual would.

Though Microraptor have the general tolerance to associate with others, many individuals choose solitary lifestyles where they are less likely to be bothered by persistent noise and bickering. This action is common in orphaned individuals, but equally, those who grew up with an unusual number of siblings may prefer the tranquility of it in contrast to their upbringing. Solitary individuals find increased happiness in following other species about, straying from their claimed carnivore to investigate other options and more frequently switching between choices on a whim. Despite this, even the most solitary Microraptor seeks occasional stimuli from others of their own kind. As such, despite often having no interest in courtship, solitary individuals may choose to gather at the courting tree within Big Tree Overlook, simply to marvel and gawk at others. Both female and male Microraptors actively choose to linger within the audience, rather than partake in courtship attempts down below. However, persistent visits may sometimes spark a reluctant interest in some otherwise solitary Microraptors, transitioning them into forming a pair when particularly impressed by a display.

Mutated Microraptor face no challenges in interacting with others of their kind, freely courting and grouping with others. However, these individuals are more often found in regions with denser foliage to avoid the effects of the sun.
Outside the below circumstances, Microraptor are generally tolerant to those outside their grouping, so long as personal space is respected.

Pairs of Microraptor and solitary individuals may claim carnivore companions, fiercely driving out rival Microraptors from approaching the same group. This applies to the entire group of carnivores, not just a sole individual. Groups of 2+ Microraptors are generally ignored by pairs, with the understanding that large clusters of their own kind do not claim companions. Microraptor become incessantly loud to grab the attention of nearby rivals once spotted. If the rivals are interested in attempting to claim the companions for themselves, they land within two body lengths of the claimed carnivore and face off with the rival, spreading their wings wide to provoke the opposing party. If the opposing party wishes to accept, they land nearby and mimic the action - at which point, a territory challenge is issued towards the opposing pair from either side. All challenge calls, including the accepting call from the opposing party, must be issued from the ground in order to make it clear to both parties that a challenge is taking place. Broadcasts and aggressive calls must be done with the natural sound of the Microraptor - mimicked calls may not be used when issuing challenges. Microraptor who are uninterested, already have claimed carnivores of their own, or have lost the challenge, move on quickly, and do not linger in the area out of spite.

When nesting, pairs of Microraptor claim individual trees or cliff ledges. Otherwise, members in a scurry claim only the general location around their nest. Microraptor only issue territory challenges to other Microraptor if their claimed space is landed on, but may begin to aggress sooner in an attempt to warn others that this is their territory. In a scurry, these challenges are still issued to signify claims. Nesting pairs, even within a scurry, do not tolerate other Microraptor close to their nest despite previous relations. Females in a harem will extend this same behaviour towards each other. Challenges are only accepted if another pair desires to use the same location for nesting. If a losing pair of Microraptor have live offspring within their nest, the parents will carry them to safety, forfeiting frequently between carrying to request the winning pair provide them with leniency. The winning pair will permit the losers to gather their chicks, but will not tolerate further aggression, and may continue to attack if provoked, potentially resulting in death.

Depending on the grouping type, Microraptor react differently to some carnivores. However, all Microraptor flee from Hatzegopteryx, Quetzalcoatlus, Megalania, Kelenken, Thalassodromeus and Tropeognathus.

Solitary or pairs of Microraptor are often tolerated by larger carnivores. These scavengers in low numbers do not draw attention to themselves, inhibit the carnivores, or place burden on the surrounding resources. Scurries are not tolerated, as too many Microraptor may draw unwanted attention to the carnivore. Microraptor only attempt to create bonds with Apex Carnivores. When attempting to bond with a larger carnivore, Microraptor does not immediately latch onto them. Upon finding a new individual they would like to bond with, Microraptor follow closely in order to acclimate the carnivore to their presence; making soft, curious chirps to hesitantly test the tolerance of the individual. Though they may attempt to remain subtle, the sound of their own wings often give them away. Over time, Microraptor close the distance, though it will not immediately latch on if this action is tolerated. Instead tolerance is regarded with some hesitancy, outweighing their interest in bonding. Microraptor are aware that even just one miscalculated move may result in serious injury, or death. After half a day's cycle has passed without aggression displayed, Microraptor begin to feel confident in having earned a carnivore’s trust enough to latch on. Should this be accepted, Microraptor chirps happily and resumes clinging to their side. If the carnivore begins to shake them off or aggresses them, Microraptor will promptly remove themself from the carnivore and silently move on to experiment with a different individual. If attempting to bond with a group of carnivores, Microraptor does not have to repeat this process with each individual. If there are both tolerant and intolerant individuals, the intolerant individuals will be avoided, with Microraptor only interacting with the tolerant. Once they are past this stage, a new relationship is formed, though this is primarily one-sided towards the Microraptor. Once permitted to latch onto their companions, Microraptor - if they have not already done so - begin to pick up on the calls of the carnivore. These calls are mimicked back at them upon being learnt. While unsure truly of what these calls mean, Microraptor test for a response and are visibly pleased when the carnivore acknowledges their efforts. Microraptor may stay bonded with their chosen companion for as long as they wish. Younger or underfed individuals often seek out different companions if they feel unsatisfied with their current. When spotting a species that Microraptor fear, individuals do not remain on their companion and instead flee and hide in nearby trees or shrubbery until the threat has passed. When their carnivore companions enter an engagement, Microraptor immediately unlatch and seek safety out of reach. They remain silent until the engagement is entirely over. Only when the engagement is finished will Microraptor latch back onto their carnivore. “Cheer Up” may then be used. Microraptor may use any of its own passive buffs on their carnivore companions prior to an engagement beginning, but may not use vocal calls as an aid before an engagement. Microraptor may not use any buff calls or attempt to assist their companions in any way during engagements and may not assist them during hunts. Microraptor may not use mimicked vocal calls during challenges to help their companion issue, accept, or forfeit challenges. Microraptor latched onto their companions grow distressed when the carnivore begins to approach the edge of deep water, unwilling to be submerged and waterlog their feathers. If the Microraptor has been bonded long enough, the tiny dromaeosaurid will cry out to persuade its companion to cross in shallower areas or areas where the crossing is narrower. Crossing large bodies of water may cause them extra distress - the unhappy Microraptor often makes their displeasure known while having to glide across. Microraptor who have experienced a companion species nesting previously may opt to time their nesting similarly - their own offspring able to disperse with the offspring of their companion, allowing offspring better success in surviving on their own. Microraptor born beside a parent’s companion species may grow to prefer this lifestyle, and rarely seek out scurries. Should a carnivore companion die in an engagement or of old age, Microraptor who have spent a considerable amount of time with the carnivore may attempt to rouse the corpse if it is not already claimed by another species. Microraptor may even use its mimicked calls or “Cheer Up” near the corpse in an attempt to receive a response from their dead companion. Nips and futile shoving at the body may occur in frustration before the Microraptor eventually gives up, forced to move on. If the body is already claimed, Microraptor seeks safety nearby and may cry out briefly, before moving on quickly. In some cases, Microraptor may even turn to their previous companion’s killer, desperately working to form a new bond.

Microraptor are known for their hyperaggression in retaliation to either themselves or their groupmates being hunted. When a member of a scurry is attacked, Microraptor will climb up high, swoop, and dive at their aggressor. The rest of the scurry - often witnessing this behavior - join in until the entire scurry is swarming the attacker. Learned vocal ability calls are not used against the attacker, their noisy defence signaled by their own broadcasts and aggressive calls during this time. Once the aggressor flees or forfeits the hunt, or is able to kill a Microraptor, the scurry will stop attacking and return to perch in high places, opting to watch their attacker’s retreat momentarily before resuming as normal. The goal is to harass the hunter until they give up, never going as far as to continue pursuing once they have left the vicinity. If intruders appear to be ignoring them, Microraptor grow relentless, scaling their intimidation display by introducing the mimicked calls of other species in retaliation. Scurries still flee from feared species and do not retaliate against Apex Carnivores, instead calling out in distress before moving out of reach.

When any species intrudes on a nesting site, both scurries and pairs react in the same way. This includes species Microraptor fear. Apex Carnivores may be excluded in this at the discretion of the Microraptor. Microraptor consider a nesting site claimed once they have courted and placed a nest in their desired location. Any species that intrudes on a claimed tree or cliff edge is met immediately with loud, screeching protests, with members swooping overhead repeatedly and aggressing the intruder. Small pecks may even be aimed at the intruder in irritation. Microraptor, towards other species, may begin to harass and aggress another species if they are within one body length of their claimed area. In scurries - even if the Microraptor has not claimed the tree or cliff edge for themselves - join in on the mobbing behavior. While assisting in defending their nesting site, Microraptor do not aggress other Microraptor from their claimed site. Pairs of Microraptor exhibit the same behavior towards species outside their claimed carnivore companions, if they have them. Microraptor are unable to issue territory or nesting challenges towards other species, as their small size does little to intimidate others. Instead, the tiny carnivore relies on harassment to deter the intruder away. If the species or individual returns within a body length, Microraptor may continue to harass.

Microraptor have an innate hatred for these species, and seek to raid their nests should they come across them, should they be at the correct hunting hunger. However, any form of physical retaliation from these groups prompt Microraptor to flee.

Up to 2 Microraptor may work together during a hunt. Microraptor may opt to hunt attended or unattended juvenile or below offspring of Deinonychus, Latenivenatrix, Psittacosaurus, and Struthiomimus. Microraptor may stalk and observe these species from a distance, tucking themselves high up into trees or cliff ledges while waiting for the opportune moment to strike. While Microraptor are relatively quiet hunters, they are extremely advantageous when it comes to using their unique ability to mimic the calls of other creatures. When working within a pair, oftentimes one Microraptor will attempt to lure adults away by mimicking calls of their own kind, serving as the perfect distraction, and allowing their partner to infiltrate the nest without issue. Equally, Microraptor may observe and utilize the calls of other species in an attempt to distract their prey into moving away from their nests. Microraptor within a scurry do not intervene or attempt to assist with calls when 2 individuals are already engaged. Instead, individuals watch silently, observing and collecting information that may prove beneficial for their next hunt. When hunting Rhamphorhynchus, tactics vastly change. Microraptor become relentless, racing in active pursuit, attempting to dive and bite at the tiny carnivore before it can flee into water. Microraptor may be attracted to the sound of herbivores, seeking out any Rhamphorhynchus that are nearby them. Even Rhamphorhynchus that are latched onto herbivores may be attacked. Microraptor do not consistently hunt the same prey and will move on after a successful hunt, not willing to risk a second encounter when their presence has already been alerted to. If Lucky Feather activates during a hunt, this is considered an individual forfeit, and the Microraptor must flee.

Microraptor gather in the south of Big Tree Overlook to court, collecting at the giant tree that looks over The Heights. Female Microraptor take positions within the branches and large roots that surround the area, silently observing the clearing below. Male Microraptor claim the clearing below as their stage, enticing onlookers by spreading their wings wide and vocalizing towards the viewing party. They compete fiercely with each other to maintain attention. When simple shoving and aggressive vocals do not work, males take part in non physical - yet highly attractive - challenges against each other, known as a showdown. Male Microraptor fortunate enough to have no competition within the clearing continue their standard displays as normal. Once a female Microraptor has made their choice in a male, she swoops down from her branch and approaches him, who continues to eagerly display his wings for her to inspect. If pleased, she will perform a short courtship dance towards him (using the ability “Cheer Up”), with the male returning the gesture if he likes her. Female Microraptors seeking a same-sex partner partake in passive courting within the audience. Bringing forth gifts and food, they approach spectating females and present the gift, mimicking a male’s display in spreading their wings. Male Microraptors seeking a same-sex partner purposefully partake in showdowns with other males, often surprising their rival when their fierce demeanour is replaced with affection and admiration. Once Microraptors have accepted a mate, they depart the courting ground together, spending the oncoming days learning the preferences and habits of their partner. Some Microraptor females are content to share the same male, forming a temporary harem group with the male and his female mates. This only occurs in scurries.

When two male Microraptor have lost patience in sharing the spotlight with each other, they perform an escalating performance of mimicry to both intimidate their rival, and further capture the audience’s attention. Facing one another, both males continue posturing by spreading their wings wide and lifting their heads to the sky. The challenge begins with one of the males vocalizing a mimicked call, always beginning with the meekest they can recall, akin to that of a small-tier species. The opposing Microraptor produces a similar call of their own in response, adhering to the tier set by the first male. If successfully met, the first male responds back, either to another call within the same tier, or escalating their mimicry to a larger tier if they have no further calls in the same tier, and the cycle continues. A male that rushes the process, either by starting with their loudest call, or not allowing for the calls to build-up appropriately, instantly lose the crowd’s favour, seen as inexperienced and immature by spectating females. The showdown continues for as long as necessary, until one male has no choice but to escalate to an apex-tier call. If one male is able to produce an apex-tier call, and the other isn’t, then the first male is deemed the winner of the showdown. If both males are able to produce a replication of an apex-tier call, it is entirely up to a female’s preference in whose performance she had been most captivated by. Female Microraptor judge by different aspects within a showdown, but commonly attractive traits are: The male able to replicate the most calls before producing an apex-tier call. The male able to produce the most unique calls, particularly from species harder to come by. After each vocalization, males posture as they await their rival’s response. A male will never replicate the same call twice in a single showdown. If at any point, a male wishes to forfeit the showdown, he will do so by fear calling and retreating a short distance, allowing for the opposing male to bask in his victory.

Microraptor nest in trees and atop cliffs, with higher seen as better and safer from predators. These sites are protected from other intruding Microraptors, in the form of a territory challenge. Harem groups place their nests relatively close to one another, but females sharing the same male will not tolerate the other female too close to her own nest. Nests are heavily decorated with items of interest, providing their future offspring with as much entertainment as possible during their youth. Clutches are small, and typically consist of only 2 eggs, where one is deemed as the main egg, and the other as a spare - in case the first does not hatch. Nesting Microraptor instinctively take on differentiating roles based on their gender. Male Microraptor are typically happier to stray further from the nest, and as such, take on the role of feeding himself, his pair and his offspring. If a male has a harem, he splits his time between the different females nesting with him and their nests. Female Microraptor take on a more observation role, staying within the general area, incubating the eggs, and only straying to collect interesting items and trinkets to further decorate the nest with.

Once eggs have hatched, parents quickly get to work drying their offspring off, preening their feathers and rewarding the chicks with attention and affection at every milestone. Parents are at their most pleased when only one of their two eggs hatch, successfully providing them with a single chick that they can dote on. In instances where the second egg hatches alongside the first, both chicks are cared for regardless, though the chick deemed as the main is prioritized, including in regards to feeding, cleaning and gifting. In rare instances, the main baby may display signs of displeasure with having to share their parent’s attention with a sibling. In some cases, but not all, the parents may choose to outcast the spare baby to provide their main baby with the best possible chances. Though cruel, parents will never go as far as directly killing their offspring. Instead, parents gently shove the spare baby out the nest, encouraging it to glide, or rather tumble, to nearby foliage, away from the nesting location. At this point, the baby will either be left completely alone, as though it were an orphan, or still cared for infrequently, fed with anything the main baby rejects. This is an opportune moment for same sex pairs to adopt an orphaned baby, and is an ideal scenario for these rejected chicks. While both parents leave frequently, offspring will rarely be left alone in the nest, unless both parents have had to leave to protect the territory from rival Microraptors. However, chicks born to a father that currently has a harem may find themselves alone every so often, as their father is forced to help care for multiple nests at once. Once chicks reach adolescence, both parents partake in encouraging further independence and flight ability. Perching on a tree, they will glide across one surface to another, waiting expectantly for their offspring to mimic them. Efforts are highly praised upon, and parents may spend several hours a day improving their chick’s mobility and confidence through games of chase. When parents feel chicks have progressed enough, they will abandon the nest, and begin slowly introducing offspring to the outside world. Still hesitant to see their offspring on the ground, many parents encourage offspring to continue moving between trees as frequently as possible. Parents showcase their offspring new pois, items, and even species, demonstrating appropriate reactions to each, and most importantly, the art of mimicry.

Once offspring reach sub-adult, parent’s reactions vary depending on if they are a pair, or a part of a scurry. If within a scurry, parents signify their lack of interest by shooing their offspring away, encouraging offspring to interact with others members of the group. Their previous affection largely disappears, though they may acknowledge kinship with an occasional affectionate call in passing. If a pair, parents will encourage their offspring to disperse, beginning with gentle shoves, and then increased aggressive display if the decision is not respected.

Same-sex paired Microraptor within scurries may adopt, often swooping in and stealing a rejected chick when they feel the urge to raise offspring. Otherwise, Microraptor do not adopt, and continuous unwanted advances into personal space are met with aggression.

Aging Microraptor begin to notice their inability to glide and fly for as long as they once were able to. Their ability to latch onto surfaces weakens, and they are more often seen tumbling to the ground, either through missing their mark, or losing significant grip strength. Some Microraptor shift their preferences in carnivore companion, preferring the territorial Tyrannosaurus or male Tyrannotitan that allows them to remain stationary. A Microraptor’s feathers may dull with age.

With their deteriorating ability to latch onto surfaces, most Microraptor find escape from predators difficult and succumb to terrestrial hunters - or are simply unable to move out of the way of passing creatures. Microraptor who can sense their waning time often seek out soft, mossy beds on the forest floor or dense underbrush to rest in, curling up to preserve any of their lasting warmth. Lifelong bonded pairs will often pass together, though when one remains alive, they will often call out in distress and attempt to rouse their passing partner.

Microraptor do not assist in the hunts of their carnivore companions. However, Microraptor may remain latched to their companion until an engagement begins. If their companion is chasing, but an engagement has not started, Microraptor may remain latched. Microraptor do not taunt hunters who have failed a hunt against them. Microraptor may not use mimicked calls to purposefully scare or trick other species except during hunts on the species they are hunting. Vocal abilities obtained through “Mimic” may not be used near engagements to avoid any side effects that typically would not occur. Microraptor may not apply vocal buffs to their carnivore companion before they enter an engagement. Microraptor may not issue or accept challenges from other species. When within LOS of an active engagement, Microraptor may not mimic the heart calls of either engaged species. If Lucky Feather activates during a hunt, this is considered an individual forfeit, and the Microraptor must flee.

Microraptor is exempt from body meshing rules while fleeing from engagements when climbing and moving on surfaces, though should not attempt to utilize meshable terrain intentionally to hide from predators. 7.2 Microraptor bites do not start an engagement unless they are hunting, or aggressing each other. 3.1 Any combination of calls, and aggressive moves, do not start a challenge against other species, and these calls can be ignored. Microraptor are unable to eat the bodies of Metriacanthosaurus without suffering adverse side effects. See 📜・server-guideOPTIONAL - Illnesses & Injuries for more information. 4.4

solo.note: Solo ist hier ganz natürlich: Laut Profil wählen viele Microraptor bewusst ein Leben allein, fern vom Gezeter der Gruppe, und dürfen sich als Einzelgänger einen Apex-Fleischfresser als Begleiter suchen. Solo heißt hier: ein kleiner Gleiter, der an der Flanke seines Riesen reitet und dessen Rufe lernt.

playstyle.summary: Du bist eine Australische Elster im Körper eines Kurzkopfgleitbeutlers: der kleinste Fleischfresser der Insel, der Stämme und Klippen hinaufklettert, von Baum zu Baum gleitet und jeden Ruf nachmacht, den er hört. Du lebst von Aas, Insekten und Kleintieren und jagst nur selten, dann aber mit List: Mit nachgeahmten Rufen lockst du Eltern von ihrem Nest weg und schnappst dir ein Küken von Deinonychus, Latenivenatrix, Psittacosaurus oder Struthiomimus, oder du hetzt einen Rhamphorhynchus, bevor er ins Wasser flüchtet. Bei der ersten Aggression fliehst du mit ängstlichem Geschrei. Solo suchst du dir einen Apex-Fleischfresser als Begleiter, reitest an seiner Seite mit und lernst seine Stimme, in der Gruppe lebst du in einem zänkischen Trupp, der jeden Angreifer gemeinsam aus der Luft attackiert.

parts.title: Alltag: Klettern, Gleiten, Nachahmen
parts.text: Wo du schlüpfst, bestimmt deine Unterart. Gui-Microraptor kommen aus den großen Wäldern, also Redwoods, Hollow Hills, Wollemi Forest, East Passage, Twisted Forest und Cedrus Forest, und haben mehr Ausdauer, wenn sie hoch in die Bäume klettern. Hanqiugi schlüpfen in Dry Fang Canyon, an den Tallbrush Coasts, den Crag Bluffs, im Coastland Swamp, in den Mudflats, an den Coastal Bluffs und auf den Palm Islands und halten länger ohne Futter und Wasser durch. Zhaoianus stammen aus Big Tree Overlook, den Wind Tunnels, Cliffedge Falls, den Black Fern Hills, den Volcano Islands und Stillwater Bog und gleiten länger. Deinen Tag verbringst du oben: Du hüpfst und gleitest von Stamm zu Stamm, klammerst dich an Klippenränder und beobachtest die Welt aus sicherer Höhe. Neue Arten beäugst du vorsichtig, und alles, was dich duldet, bekommt seine eigenen Rufe zurück, manchmal als ganze Unterhaltung, manchmal ahmst du sogar seine Bewegungen nach, bis es genervt wirkt. Du merkst dir jede Stimme und jede Begegnung. Du sammelst Fundstücke, nimmst sie ins Visier und schleppst sie herum, auch wenn sie meist zu schwer sind. Wasser magst du nicht, sauber bist du trotzdem: Auf sandigen Lichtungen und Ufern nimmst du Staubbäder und wirfst den Sand mit der Schnauze hoch. Du schläfst in kurzen Etappen und immer hoch oben in einem Baum oder an einer Klippe, nie in Höhlen oder Tunneln. Hast du einen Begleiter, folgst du ihm erst mit leisem Zirpen, bis er dich einen halben Tag lang geduldet hat, dann klammerst du dich an seine Seite und schläfst dort auch auf Wanderungen. Schüttelt er dich ab, ziehst du still weiter. Am tiefen Wasser zeterst du, bis er eine seichte oder schmale Stelle nimmt. Von Metriacanthosaurus-Kadavern wird dir übel.

parts.title: Jagd & Gefahr
parts.text: Meist frisst du Aas, Insekten und Kleintiere. Jagen darfst du nur Jungtiere bis Juvenile von Deinonychus, Latenivenatrix, Psittacosaurus und Struthiomimus, auch wenn die Eltern danebenstehen, außerdem Rhamphorhynchus, und das höchstens zu zweit. Deinonychus und Latenivenatrix hasst du, ihre Nester plünderst du, wenn du hungrig genug bist, doch jede körperliche Gegenwehr schlägt dich in die Flucht. Du lauerst hoch im Baum oder auf einem Felsvorsprung und wartest auf den richtigen Moment. Zu zweit lockt einer die Eltern mit ihren eigenen nachgeahmten Rufen weg, während der andere ins Nest schlüpft, allein lenkst du die Beute mit den Rufen anderer Arten ab. Rhamphorhynchus jagst du dagegen offen, stürzt dich im Gleitflug auf ihn, bevor er ins Wasser entkommt, und greifst ihn sogar auf einem Pflanzenfresser an. Nach einem Erfolg ziehst du weiter. Löst Lucky Feather aus, hast du aufgegeben und musst fliehen. Vor Hatzegopteryx, Quetzalcoatlus, Megalania, Kelenken, Thalassodromeus und Tropeognathus fliehst du immer, außer am Nest, und vor allem, was du nicht jagen darfst, fliehst du allein oder zu zweit. Kämpft dein Begleiter, springst du ab und bleibst still, du hilfst ihm nie und setzt vorher keine Rufe als Buff ein. Nachgeahmte Rufe benutzt du nie, um andere zu erschrecken, außer bei der eigenen Jagd. Im Trupp stürzt ihr euch auf jeden Jäger, außer Apex-Fleischfresser, bis er aufgibt. Wer euren Nestbaum betritt, wird von allen angekreischt, umkreist und gezwickt.

parts.title: Partnersuche & Balz
parts.text: Die Balz läuft wie im Profil am riesigen Baum im Süden von Big Tree Overlook, der über The Heights blickt. Weibchen sitzen still in den Ästen und Wurzeln, Männchen spreizen auf der Lichtung darunter die Flügel und rufen. Werden zwei Männchen ungeduldig, kommt es zum Showdown: Sie ahmen abwechselnd Rufe nach, beginnend mit der leisesten kleinen Art und Stufe für Stufe größer, bis einer einen Apex-Ruf bringen muss. Wer überstürzt, verliert die Gunst des Publikums, und kein Ruf darf doppelt kommen. Gefällt einem Weibchen ein Männchen, gleitet sie herab und tanzt mit Cheer Up, er antwortet, wenn er sie mag. Gleichgeschlechtliche Weibchen werben im Publikum mit Geschenken, Männchen über den Showdown. Harems gibt es nur im Trupp. Genistet wird hoch in Bäumen oder auf Klippen, das Nest wird mit Fundstücken geschmückt, und in beiden Jahreszeiten gibt es 2 Eier pro 2 Stunden: ein Hauptei und ein Ersatzei. Das Männchen füttert, das Weibchen brütet. Ein ungeliebtes Ersatzküken kann aus dem Nest geschubst werden, getötet wird es nie.

methodology.intent: Profile-specific hunt, prey, rivalry and avoidance rules are checked before tier eligibility.
methodology.pursuit: Relevant land, water or flight caps and sprint duration determine whether contact can be forced.
methodology.groups: By default you are solo and the other side brings its full legal group; both sides can be set to any size up to the profile caps. Unlimited groups are never turned into an invented number.
methodology.fight: Every hit is resolved as damage × (attacker CW ÷ victim CW) ÷ victim armour from the adult stat curves. Each side focus-fires one target at a time with its best spammable attack plus up to two stronger abilities. Times assume every swing lands, so agile, smaller players outperform them by dodging. Bleed stacks, ignores armour and blocks healing; it is shown as pressure and only converted into health when you switch on the estimate, because that rate is not documented.
methodology.encounter: Mapped area overlap lowers or raises relevance, but an explicit cross-species rule can override sparse map overlap.

analog.label: Australian magpie + Sugar glider
analog.headline: An Australian magpie in a sugar glider's body: a tiny glider that copies every call, remembers every face and dive-bombs anything near its nest tree.
analog.playsLike: You are the smallest carnivore on the roster (Tiny, 500 combat weight, 400 HP, a 40 bite that only hurts targets under 600 combat weight, land sprint 825 for 400 s). You climb trunks and cliffs, glide from tree to tree and sleep in short bursts high up, never in caves. You live on carrion, insects and critters and hunt only Juvenile-and-younger Deinonychus, Latenivenatrix, Psittacosaurus and Struthiomimus, even guarded ones, plus Rhamphorhynchus, with at most one partner. Your weapon is mimicry: copied calls lure the parents away from their nest. In a scurry of up to 10 you swarm and dive-bomb anything that hunts you, except Apex carnivores and the six species you always flee from; as a pair or alone you may claim an Apex carnivore as your companion, ride on its side and learn its calls.

setting.label: Tree canopy and cliff ledges across most of the island
setting.note: Hatches all over the island; the subspecies follows the birth POI (Gui in the big forests, Hanqiugi on the coasts, swamps and in Dry Fang Canyon, Zhaoianus around Big Tree Overlook, the cliffs and the bog). Lives in trees and on cliff ledges, never in caves, and courts at the giant tree in the south of Big Tree Overlook.

analogs.covers: Voice and temper: a brilliant mimic with a long memory for faces that swoops screeching at anything near its nest tree and lives in noisy, bickering groups
Body and movement: a palm-sized climber that glides from trunk to trunk, sleeps high in the trees and rests together with its colony

why.text: Microraptor “are most commonly known for their mimicry of other species” and parrot calls back at tolerant species in “conversations”. Australian magpies are among the best vocal mimics, copying other birds, dogs and even sirens.

They “have an excellent memory, often recalling not only calls they’ve heard, but past experiences they have had with certain species”. Australian magpies recognise individual people for years and swoop only at the ones they remember as a threat.

Any intruder on a claimed nest tree is “met immediately with loud, screeching protests, with members swooping overhead repeatedly”: the magpie's swooping season, with small pecks included (official inspiration: magpies).

Microraptor “spend most of their time hopping and gliding from tree to tree or clinging to the edges of cliffs”. Sugar gliders cross the canopy the same way and sleep high up in tree hollows (official inspiration: sugar gliders).
In a scurry “all Microraptor take time to rest in unison”, like a sugar glider colony asleep in one hollow.

The clutch holds a main egg and “a spare - in case the first does not hatch”, and a favoured chick may get its sibling pushed out of the nest: the insurance egg of the Nazca booby (official inspiration).

notLike: Australian magpies walk and fly; Microraptor climbs, glides and only hops about on the ground.
Magpie groups defend a large territory all year; Microraptor claims only its nest tree, a cliff ledge or its carnivore companion, and flees at the first sign of aggression.
Sugar gliders are nocturnal and live on sap and nectar; Microraptor is cathemeral and lives on carrion, insects and critters.
analog.twist: A whole songbird brain packed into the smallest predator on the island: mimicry is its weapon, its courtship and its small talk.
analog.officialInspiration: rats, gray squirrels, sugar gliders, magpies, nazca boobies, and creative liberty

analog.label: Fork-tailed drongo + Sugar glider
analog.headline: A drongo that has picked a giant: you ride an Apex carnivore, copy its calls, live off its leftovers and glide off into the trees when it gets dangerous.
analog.playsLike: Alone you choose an Apex carnivore as your companion. You follow it with soft chirps until it has tolerated you for half a day, then you latch onto its side, ride along and learn its calls. You never help it: when it enters an engagement you let go, hide silently and only cheer it up afterwards. You eat carrion, insects and critters, hunt Juvenile-and-younger Deinonychus, Latenivenatrix, Psittacosaurus and Struthiomimus with copied calls as a lure, and chase Rhamphorhynchus. You flee from anything you cannot hunt and from Hatzegopteryx, Quetzalcoatlus, Megalania, Kelenken, Thalassodromeus and Tropeognathus. Other Microraptor near your companion get a ground challenge in your own voice.

setting.label: Tree canopy and cliff ledges across most of the island
setting.note: Hatches all over the island; the subspecies follows the birth POI (Gui in the big forests, Hanqiugi on the coasts, swamps and in Dry Fang Canyon, Zhaoianus around Big Tree Overlook, the cliffs and the bog). Lives in trees and on cliff ledges, never in caves, and courts at the giant tree in the south of Big Tree Overlook.

analogs.covers: Solo life: a lone rider that attaches itself to a big animal, copies its calls and lives off what it stirs up and leaves behind
Body and movement: a palm-sized climber that glides from trunk to trunk and sleeps in short bursts high in the trees

why.text: Solitary Microraptor “may claim a carnivore companion” and “only attempt to create bonds with Apex Carnivores”. Fork-tailed drongos attach themselves to meerkats, babblers and big grazers and follow them all day.
Once allowed to latch on, it begins to “pick up on the calls of the carnivore” and mimics them back. Drongos copy the calls of the animals they live with.
On a hunt it may “utilize the calls of other species in an attempt to distract their prey”, the way a drongo's false alarm calls make meerkats drop their food.
Solitary Microraptor find “increased happiness in following other species about” and switch companions “on a whim”, just as drongos change hosts during the day.
It still lives up high: it sleeps in short bursts “always high up in a tree or cliff”, as a sugar glider does.

notLike: Drongos are fearless and mob eagles; a Microraptor flees at the first sign of aggression and leaves its companion the moment an engagement starts.
Drongos catch insects in flight; Microraptor glides from trunk to trunk and finds its food on the ground and in the trees.

solo.summary: Solo bist du ein Trauerdrongo, der sich einen Riesen ausgesucht hat. Du folgst einem Apex-Fleischfresser mit leisem Zirpen, bis er dich einen halben Tag geduldet hat, dann klammerst du dich an seine Seite, reitest mit und lernst seine Rufe. In seine Kämpfe und Jagden mischst du dich nie ein: Beginnt ein Kampf, springst du ab, versteckst dich still und munterst ihn erst danach mit Cheer Up auf. Du lebst von Aas, Insekten und Kleintieren, lockst mit nachgeahmten Rufen Eltern von ihren Küken weg und jagst Rhamphorhynchus im Gleitflug. Andere Microraptor an deinem Begleiter forderst du am Boden mit deiner eigenen Stimme heraus. Geschlafen wird in kurzen Etappen hoch oben im Baum, an der Klippe oder an der Flanke deines Riesen.
